context: typical-floor cycle · emerging vertical MEP spine (risers, fire alarm)

brief.intro: Mid-rise residential covers buildings from about ground plus four to ground plus nine storeys — tall enough to need a lift and a coordinated vertical MEP spine (risers, fire alarm, sometimes a light wet riser), but not yet tall enough for the full life-safety and pumping infrastructure of a high-rise. The structure repeats a typical floor, much like an apartment building, but now the shared cores and shafts genuinely drive sequencing: risers must be built in step with the structural cycle, tested floor by floor, and protected while finishing trades pass through. This is the transition band of residential construction — finishing still does most of the work, but vertical services coordination stops being optional and starts appearing on the critical path if it isn't planned in step with the floor cycle.

must_get_right: Build the riser in step with the structural cycle — a shaft that falls behind blocks every unit above it, not just one floor.
Pressure- and function-test each floor's riser section before it's boxed in — retesting after enclosure is far more disruptive.
Plan fire-alarm zoning and cause-and-effect testing early — it's a real commissioning activity here, not a same-day snag item.
Sequence the finishing wave a fixed number of floors behind structure — close enough to keep pace, far enough to avoid clashing with riser testing.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Structure and civil run a standard 6-day working calendar; MEP and finishing trades may add a second shift at peak to keep the finishing wave behind the floor cycle. Riser installation and testing stay within the normal calendar rather than extended shifts, since they need continuous supervision.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The typical-floor structural cycle sets the earliest riser-install date per floor. Once the riser front falls in behind structure it becomes the true governing path, because every unit above depends on a tested, closed riser section. Finishing follows in a rolling wave a fixed number of floors behind the riser front, with fire-alarm zoning and cause-and-effect testing at the back end.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design and a sample/mock-up unit are approved before the floor-cycle rollout begins; the riser subcontractor is mobilised in step with the structural crane cycle; a single mobilisation; handover proceeds by floor-band.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The following are tracked as milestones and drive the network:

rows: Wet riser fire pump set (where required)

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Tower crane time is shared across structure, riser materials and cladding delivery; the riser shaft has restricted access while the structural crew works above; floor-band access must be coordinated for phased handover; noise and working-hour limits often apply near occupied neighbours.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: riser installation or testing slippage compounding up the building, fire-alarm zoning rework if not designed floor-by-floor early, and lift delivery delay blocking upper-floor access. Contingency is held at the riser-to-finishing transition and before phased handover rather than spread across floors.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (floor-band summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 (floor-by-floor); expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead by unit/trade for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
